title: Made in Vadodara, Flown by the Air Force: India's First Privately Built Military Aircraft Is Ready
excerpt: The rollout of a Tata-built Airbus C-295 transport plane from a Gujarat factory floor marks a quiet revolution in Indian defence manufacturing — and a vindication of the bet that private industry can build warplanes.
body:
The first Airbus C-295 military transport aircraft assembled entirely on Indian soil is ready for rollout at Tata Advanced Systems Limited's facility in Vadodara, Gujarat. It is not a fighter jet. It is not a stealth drone. It is a sturdy, unglamorous workhorse designed to carry 71 soldiers or 9,000 kilograms of cargo to remote airstrips. And yet, this aircraft may be the most significant thing India's private defence sector has ever produced.

## Why this matters

India has built military hardware before — Hindustan Aeronautics Limited has produced the Tejas light combat aircraft and the Dhruv helicopter. But those were public-sector projects, shepherded by a state-owned monopoly with decades of institutional knowledge and, critics would add, decades of delays. The C-295 is different. This is a Tata Group company, working with Airbus Defence and Space under a Rs 21,935-crore contract signed in 2021, delivering a fully assembled military aircraft from a privately run production line.

The deal calls for 56 C-295s for the Indian Air Force. Sixteen have already been delivered directly from Airbus's plant in Seville, Spain. The remaining 40 are to be manufactured in Vadodara, with progressively increasing Indian content. The aircraft rolling out now is the first of that Indian-built batch — and it carries over 13,000 domestically sourced components.

## The ecosystem effect

The Vadodara facility is not just an assembly line. It has spawned a supplier ecosystem of more than 125 Indian MSMEs providing avionics sub-assemblies, wiring harnesses, structural components and tooling. For a country that still imports roughly 65 per cent of its defence equipment, the C-295 programme represents a working proof of concept for the Atmanirbhar Bharat initiative that the government has championed since 2020.

Defence analysts have been cautiously optimistic. The C-295 is not a cutting-edge platform — it is a turboprop transport aircraft that competes with the Brazilian Embraer C-390 and the Italian Leonardo C-27J. But that is precisely the point. India needs volume manufacturing experience before it can credibly pursue more complex programmes like the Advanced Medium Combat Aircraft or the Indian Multi-Role Helicopter.

## The Avro replacement saga

The C-295 replaces the Avro HS-748, an aircraft that entered IAF service in the 1960s and has been limping along well past its design life. Several Avros have been grounded for structural fatigue; at least two were involved in incidents blamed on metal fatigue in the past decade. The replacement programme was first mooted in 2009. That it took 17 years from concept to Indian rollout tells you everything about the pace of defence procurement in New Delhi.

## What the diaspora should watch

For the Indian-origin aerospace engineers who populate Boeing, Airbus, Lockheed Martin and Rolls-Royce facilities from Toulouse to Wichita, the C-295 programme is both a source of pride and a potential career inflection point. Tata has been quietly recruiting experienced NRI engineers, offering relocation packages and leadership roles that would be rare at Western OEMs. The Vadodara facility's quality standards, certified to AS9100D, are designed to be internationally interoperable, meaning work done here counts toward global aerospace credentials.

India's defence export ambitions add another dimension. The government has set a target of Rs 50,000 crore in defence exports by 2029. A working C-295 production line gives India a platform it can offer to friendly nations — the aircraft's short-takeoff capability makes it suitable for Southeast Asian, African and Latin American air forces with rudimentary airfield infrastructure.

## The quiet revolution

No one will mistake the C-295 for a glamorous programme. It will not feature in Top Gun sequels or generate breathless cable news coverage. But manufacturing a military aircraft at scale, with private capital and a domestic supply chain, is the kind of foundational capability that transforms defence industries. India has taken a very long time to get here. The plane, at least, is finally ready.
